Author: @xoppa09
Content:
"Completing the square" means algebraically that you can add (b/2)²  to the expression x²  + bx  to get a perfect square, namely  ( x + b / 2 ) ²  . You can verify that ( x + b / 2 ) ² is equal to x² + bx + (b/2)²  by multiplying out ( x + b / 2 ) ² using "Foil" (first outer inner last) and collecting like terms. 
The video is a nice 'geometric proof' of this process, and historically the term completing the square derives from this. Note that the negative solution falls out of the algebra, while it does not fall out of the geometric model (quadratic equations can have two distinct solutions). I don't think this bothered ancient mathematicians because they did not take negative integers seriously until the Renaissance (even though the arithmetic of negative integers has a real world analogy, the arithmetic of debts). 

So say we start with the equation x² + bx = k.
We can 'complete the square' by adding the appropriate constant to both sides of the equation that results in the left side becoming a perfect square. 

x² + bx = k
x² + bx + (b/2)² = k + (b/2)²
(x+b/2)² = k + (b/2)²
x + b/2 = ± √( k + (b/2)² )
x = - b/2  ± √ (k + (b/2)² ) . 
The symbol ±  is a condensed notation for plus or minus, since the square root of a number has two solutions, positive and negative. Therefore the two solutions are x = - b/2  + √ (k + (b/2)² )  and x = - b/2  - √ (k + (b/2)² ) .

Similar with "imaginary" numbers I prefer to think of them as "perpendicular" numbers.

If we consider (Z, +) as a structure, we observe that 1 has the inverse -1, 2 has the inverse -2, and so forth. Because vector spaces can only be defined over fields, negative numbers form an essential component of the mathematical description of our reality.
Thus, subtraction is not truly a distinct arithmetic operation but rather addition with the additive inverse. This fundamental concept is introduced already in introductory courses on linear algebra.

Author: @basharic3162
Content:
I'm a print designer. Newspapers specifically. Not a math geek. This reminds me of something from my youth.

I was well versed in the dominant page layout program of the day (QuarkExpress), but took it upon myself to to grab one of those "Bible" books on the chance I'd missed some wrinkle here or there. The important nugget of information needed for this story is Quark allows you to draw a text frame and set how many columns of type you'd like in the frame. If you make the frame wider your columns get wider too. You can also set the size of the gap between columns that will stay at what you set. 

I remember the author of the bible book going through a hypothetical where you had to place a large number of mugshot pictures on a page. He went through this long, drawn out math routine to arrive at what size each mugshot should be.

Instead I drew two text frames and set the columns on one for how many mugs I wanted going across. The other I set for how many mugs I wanted going down, then rotated that box 90 degrees. I sized each to the page one on top of the other giving me a perfect grid of guide lines showing me where to put each mugshot. That takes about 30 seconds to do. 

The TLDR is to never underestimate the power of good old-fashioned figgerin' for solving problems.
